q: 101. Refractory bricks are specially manufactured
options: to have high insulation against sound
explain: Refractory bricks, also known as fire bricks, are designed to resist high temperatures (up to 1700°C) without melting or softening.

q: 102. The soil good for making bricks is
explain: Clayey soil is ideal because it provides the necessary plasticity for molding and strength after burning.

q: 103. The impurity not desirable in the soil used for brick formation is
explain: Alkalis cause efflorescence (white staining), while Kankar (lime nodules) can cause bricks to split upon hydration.

q: 104. The ingredient of the brick earth which enables the brick to retain shape is
explain: Silica prevents the brick from warping, shrinking, and cracking; it provides the 'skeleton' for shape retention.

q: 105. The maximum percentage of ingredients in brick formation is
explain: Silica (sand) constitutes the largest portion of brick earth, typically ranging from 50% to 60%.

q: 106. Percentage of silica in a good brick earth lies between
explain: For a good brick earth, silica should be present in the range of 50-60% to ensure durability and prevent shrinkage.

q: 107. The red colour of the brick is due to
explain: Iron oxide (roughly 5-6%) acts as a flux and imparts the characteristic red color to the brick upon burning.

q: 108. The standard size of a brick as per Nepal Standard (NS) is
explain: The Nepal Standard (NS) specifies the brick size as 230mm x 115mm x 57mm.

q: 109. During compressive strength load is applied at the rate of
explain: Standard testing procedures require the load to be applied at a steady rate of 14 N/mm² per minute until failure.

q: 110. The percentage of alumina in good brick earth lies between
explain: Alumina is responsible for plasticity and should be between 20-30% of the brick earth volume.

q: 111. Excess of silica in brick earth causes
explain: While silica is vital, an excess makes the brick brittle and weak because it destroys the cohesion between soil particles.

q: 112. Excess of alumina in a brick earth causes
explain: Excess alumina makes the clay too plastic, leading to significant shrinkage, cracking, and warping during the drying and burning process.

q: 113. The main function of alumina in brick earth is
explain: Alumina absorbs water and renders the clay plastic, which is essential for the molding of the brick.

q: 114. The process of mixing clay, water and other ingredients to make brick is called
explain: Tempering is the process of adding water to the brick earth and kneading it to achieve a uniform, plastic mass.

q: 115. The process of mixing sand with the powdered natural soil to improve the quality is known as
explain: Blending involves adding specific materials (like sand or chalk) to the clay to correct its composition before molding.

q: 116. Excess of iron oxide in brick earth causes
options: the colour change i.e. from red to dark blue
explain: While iron oxide provides the red color, an excess amount during burning causes the brick to turn dark blue or blackish.

q: 117. Lime is mixed with brick earth
explain: Lime in brick earth helps the silica to fuse at a lower temperature and prevents the raw bricks from shrinking and warping.

q: 118. The maximum percentage of water absorption of 1st class bricks in 24 hrs should be limited to
explain: High-quality 1st class bricks should not absorb more than 1/6th of their dry weight (approximately 15%) when immersed in water for 24 hours.

q: 119. The maximum percentage of water absorption of 2nd class bricks in 24 hrs should be limited to
explain: For 2nd class bricks, the standard allowable limit for water absorption is 20% of its dry weight.

q: 120. The crushing strength of 1st class brick should not be less than
explain: 1st class bricks are required to have a minimum compressive (crushing) strength of 10.5 N/mm² or 105 kg/cm².

q: 121. The minimum compressive strength of a 2nd class bricks should be
explain: 2nd class bricks must have a minimum crushing strength of 7.0 N/mm² or 70 kg/cm².

q: 122. The temperature at which bricks are burnt varies from (low melting clay)
explain: Standard bricks are typically burnt in a kiln at temperatures ranging between 700°C and 1000°C depending on the clay type.

q: 123. For one cubic meter of brick masonry, the number of machine made brick required as per NS is
explain: According to Nepal Standards, approximately 530 machine-made bricks are required to complete 1 cubic meter of masonry.

q: 124. The number of standard bricks required for one cubic meter of brick masonry (IS standard) is
explain: For standard modular bricks (19cm x 9cm x 9cm), the nominal requirement including mortar is 500 bricks per cubic meter.

q: 125. The red colour obtained by the bricks is due to the presence of
explain: Iron oxide is the primary chemical ingredient responsible for the characteristic red hue of burnt clay bricks.

q: 126. The soil used for the manufacture of bricks should preferably not contain the following material
explain: Pebbles and stones prevent the uniform mixing of clay and can cause the brick to crack during the burning process.

q: 127. Tiles are used for
explain: Clay tiles are versatile components used for roofing, flooring, and constructing drainage conduits.

q: 128. The amount of local brick required for one m3 masonry (As per NS norms)
explain: Due to size variations in local traditional bricks in Nepal, the norm usually estimates 560 bricks per cubic meter.

q: 129. The internal size of mould used in brick preparation is
options: smaller than the size of fully burnt brick
larger than the size of fully burnt brick
equal to the size of fully burnt brick
explain: Moulds are made 8-10% larger than the desired brick size to account for the shrinkage that occurs during drying and burning.

q: 130. If fine sand or ash is sprinkled on the inner surface of mould, the bricks are known as
explain: Sprinkling sand inside the mould helps the clay block slide out easily; these are specifically called sand-moulded bricks.

q: 131. Pug mill is used for
explain: A pug mill is used for 'pugging,' which is the process of kneading the clay to make it uniform and plastic for moulding.

q: 132. Advantage of clamp burning as compared to kiln burning is
options: when large number of bricks are required
explain: Clamps are temporary structures and do not require the expensive permanent construction associated with kilns.

q: 133. The over ground continuous kiln is
explain: Hoffman's kiln is a permanent, over-ground continuous kiln, whereas Bull's Trench is typically partially underground.

q: 134. Hoffman's kiln is a
explain: Hoffman's kilns allow for continuous loading, burning, and unloading of bricks in different chambers simultaneously.

q: 135. Which brick is adopted well ?
explain: A high-quality brick must possess all these physical characteristics: high strength, proper burning, and low porosity.

q: 136. The bricks used for lining of furnaces is
explain: Refractory (fire) bricks are specifically made to withstand the intense heat inside furnaces and chimneys.

q: 137. Fire bricks should be laid in a
explain: To maintain thermal consistency, fire bricks are laid using fire clay mortar which can resist similar high temperatures.

q: 138. In bricks masonry, the frog of the brick generally kept on
explain: The 'frog' (indentation) is placed facing up so that it can be filled with mortar, creating a mechanical key with the course above.

q: 139. Bull nose bricks are not used in
explain: Bullnose bricks have rounded edges and are used for corners or pillars, but they are not standard for arch construction.

q: 140. Hollow bricks are used for
explain: The air trapped inside hollow bricks acts as an excellent thermal insulator, keeping interiors cooler in summer and warmer in winter.

q: 141. Fire bricks are used
explain: Refractory bricks have low thermal conductivity, helping to contain heat within a furnace and decrease outward heat flow.

q: 142. Terracotta is used in building for
explain: Terracotta is a glazed or unglazed fired clay used primarily for decorative architectural elements and ornamental work.

q: 143. Bloating of bricks is due to
options: presence of excess carbonaceous matter and sulphur
presence of any gas forming material in clay
explain: Bloating is a spongy swollen mass caused by the entrapped gases from carbonaceous matter and sulphur during firing.

q: 144. Swelling of bricks is known as
explain: Bloating is the term for the permanent swelling of a brick, often caused by internal gas pressure during burning.

q: 145. The quantity of sand in brick is about
explain: Silica (sand) typically makes up about 50-60% of brick earth, which is roughly equivalent to 3/5ths.

q: 146. The bricks are properly soaked in water before use the following reason
options: to wash the kiln dust for better bondage with mortar
to avoid the chances of absorption of water from the mortar
to spread the mortar uniformly between them
explain: Soaking ensures the bricks don't suck water from the mortar (which weakens it) and removes dust for better adhesion.

q: 147. In one day, the height of brick masonry construction should generally not exceed
explain: To prevent the fresh mortar in lower courses from being crushed by the weight of new work, the daily height is limited to 1m.

q: 148. Frog means
explain: In masonry terminology, a frog is the depression or indentation made on the top face of a brick.

q: 149. For manufacture of bricks normally the top soil is removed having a depth of .....
explain: The top 20cm of soil is usually stripped away (unsoiling) as it contains organic matter and impurities unsuitable for bricks.

q: 150. Tampering of soil for manufacture of bricks, is done by
explain: Kneading the soil (tempering) can be done manually by feet, using cattle, or mechanically in a pug mill.

q: 151. In case of clamp for burning of bricks, the bricks/ fuel are laid at a slope of...
explain: Clamps are constructed with a slight inward slope, usually around 15 degrees, to ensure stability as the fuel burns away.

q: 152. Normally the bricks (1st class) obtained from pazawah is about
explain: Pazawah (clamp) burning is less efficient than kiln burning, typically yielding about 60% good quality bricks.

q: 153. The top and sides of a clamp (pazawah) is plastered with mud and cow dung to prevent.....
explain: Plastering the exterior of the clamp acts as insulation to retain the internal heat required for proper burning.

q: 154. Lamination of bricks is caused due to
options: entrapped air in the voids of the clay
entrapped water in the voids of the clay
explain: Lamination occurs when air is trapped within the clay during machine moulding, creating thin layers or planes of weakness.

q: 155. Strike is used to remove the
explain: A strike is a wooden or metal straight-edge used to scrape off excess clay from the top of the mould.

q: 156. Refractory bricks are used in
explain: Refractory bricks are essential for lining combustion chambers where temperatures are extremely high.

q: 157. Refractory bricks are
explain: Refractory bricks are categorized into three types—acidic, basic, and neutral—based on their chemical resistance to slag.

q: 158. Generally wooden moulds are made from
explain: Hardwoods like Shisham are preferred for brick moulds because they resist wear and warping from moisture.

q: 159. Choose the correct statement
options: percentage of silica is increased in 1st class brick
percentage of alumina is increased in refractory brick
percentage of alumina is increased in 1st class brick
explain: Refractory bricks require a higher percentage of alumina (and silica) to withstand extreme temperatures without melting.

q: 160. If rain water falls on hot bricks then the shape of the brick gets deformed, this defect is known as
explain: Chuffs is the defect caused when falling rain hits hot, newly burnt bricks, resulting in cracking and deformation.

q: 161. The discolouration and formation of white deposits due to presence of relatively large proportion of soluble salts in a bricks is known as
explain: Efflorescence is the white powdery deposit left on a brick surface when moisture evaporates and leaves behind soluble salts.

q: 162. Dolomite bricks are
explain: Dolomite is a basic material; therefore, bricks made from it are classified as basic refractory bricks.

q: 163. Jhumb bricks
explain: Jhumb bricks (or Jhama bricks) are over-burnt bricks that have become vitrified and often distorted in shape.

q: 164. Second class bricks
options: produce a metallic sound when struck
explain: While 2nd class bricks may have slight irregularities, they should still be well-burnt and produce a metallic ringing sound.

q: 165. The reason for the popularity of bricks as construction material is that
options: they are cheap and available locally at all places
they are durable and possess fairly good strength and lighter than stones
they have very good insulating property against heat and sound
explain: Bricks are widely used due to their cost-effectiveness, durability, ease of handling, and natural insulation properties.

q: 166. The most widely used kiln in Nepal is
explain: Bull's Trench Kiln is the most popular type in Nepal due to its cost-efficiency and ability to produce a large volume of bricks continuously.

q: 167. The standard size of brick as per Indian standard is
explain: The standard modular brick size as per IS: 1077 is 19 cm x 9 cm x 9 cm.

q: 168. The soil used for the manufacture of bricks should preferably not contain the following material
explain: Alkalies cause efflorescence, while pebbles and kankar lead to cracking and weakness in the finished brick.

q: 169. The maximum percentages of fine sand content in soil for making good tiles is about
explain: Good tile earth requires a specific balance, typically capped at 40% fine sand to maintain structural integrity.

q: 170. The maximum percentages of clay content for making good tiles, is about
explain: Clay provides the necessary plasticity for molding tiles, and for high-quality production, it is usually limited to around 30%.

q: 171. The maximum percentages of silt content for making good tiles, is about
explain: Silt content is kept moderate (around 30%) to ensure the tile does not become too brittle after firing.

q: 172. The maximum percentages of warping along the sides of tiles, is
explain: Quality control standards for tiles generally allow for a maximum of 2% warping along the edges.

q: 173. which one is correct ?
options: quick lime generates heat on water addition
quick lime is obtained by calcination of pure lime
explain: All the statements are characteristics of quick lime (Calcium Oxide); it slakes rapidly, produces heat (exothermic), and is derived from calcining limestone.

q: 174. The main constituents, which is mainly responsible for hydraulicity is
explain: The presence of clay (silicates of alumina) is the primary factor that gives lime the ability to set under water (hydraulicity).

q: 175. Which one is correct?
options: consistency test is done at a temperature of 25°C to 29°C
consistency & setting time for a concrete is obtained by vicat's apparatus
explain: These are standard specifications: 27° ± 2°C is the ideal curing temperature, and the Vicat's apparatus is the standard tool for consistency/setting time tests.
